Session 06 · M05 · Hypothesis tests, effect size & A/B decisions

Test the claim before you ship it

State hypotheses before the data arrive, read a p-value for what it is, and weigh effect size, guardrails and net impact before recommending a rollout.

Before class

Readiness check

Three questions, one minute. Your score suggests a path through the lesson.

Take the check
1. A test of H₀ (no difference) gives p = 0.03 with α = 0.05. What follows?

Correct. The p-value describes the data under H₀; with p below α you reject H₀.

A p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true. It is not the probability that H₀ is true.

Significance says the difference is unlikely to be noise. Size and value are separate questions.

2. Version B lifts conversion from 40% to 50%. How big is the lift?

Correct. 50% − 40% = 10 percentage points. In relative terms that is a 25% lift.

25% is the relative lift (10 ÷ 40), and it is a percent, not percentage points.

The gap between two rates is measured in percentage points. In relative terms it is 25%.

3. A very large test finds a significant lift of 0.1 points that costs more than it earns. What do you recommend?

Large samples make tiny effects significant. Check whether the effect pays for itself.

Correct. Weigh the effect size, guardrails and net impact before deciding.

Rerunning until p shrinks inflates false positives and ignores the cost question.

By the end of this session

You can

  • State H₀ and H₁ and choose a two-sided test before looking at the results.
  • Compute and interpret t and z statistics, p-values and a confidence interval for a difference.
  • Decide with practical significance, guardrail metrics and net business impact, not the p-value alone.
